weaknesses: Finite-sample framing oversells what the constants deliver (abstract, introduction, the titles of the two main theorems, and 'Statistical implications'). By the paper's own algorithm the polynomial-correction branch is active only when log(e+n) >= 128, i.e. n above roughly e^128, and the upper constant contains C_fall = 4e^128. So at every attainable sample size the estimator is the arrived-outcome contrast, and the interval radius sqrt(C_U r/alpha) clips to [-1,1]. The Limitations paragraph on 'practical constants' is too soft to convey this. Fix: state in the introduction and after the estimator definition that the characterization is a rate result with uniform but very large constants, name the activation threshold explicitly, and retitle the theorems as rate characterizations (e.g. 'Minimax risk rate') or add a remark giving the regime in which the correction is active.

The surrogate has no role in the rate, and the paper never says so. The benchmark is free of any surrogate quantity, the converse uses a constant surrogate (noted only in passing in 'Statistical implications'), and the estimator treats S as a cell coordinate that merely multiplies the cell count. Yet the abstract, introduction and related work position the paper next to surrogate-assisted identification (Kallus and Mao). Fix: add a paragraph in 'Statistical implications' stating that the minimax rate coincides with that of the model without a surrogate, that S enters only by weakening MAR to conditioning on (X,A,S), and that the surrogate-specific efficiency gains of Kallus and Mao are invisible at this rate resolution.

The honest interval is a fixed-width Markov interval and the paper should say so when it claims optimality. Its radius is deterministic, depends on the law class only through (n,d,q), and scales as alpha^{-1/2}. The length theorem holds only for fixed alpha, with untracked dependence of c_alpha and C_alpha on alpha. A reader may take 'attains the length bound' as a usable inference procedure. Fix: in the paragraph after the interval definition and in 'Statistical implications', state that the optimal worst-law length is attained by a non-adaptive radius, that law-adaptive shortening is outside the criterion, and that the alpha-dependence of the upper and lower constants differs (alpha^{-1/2} against a factor of order 1-2alpha).

The restrictions that carry the result are stated but not motivated in the main text. (a) q in [1/2,1] is imposed without explaining where the proof uses it (w_j <= 2*delta*t_j in the upper bound, validity of the prior's outcome means in the converse); it is discussed only in Limitations. (b) Exactly balanced, known assignment is essential for dimension-free precision at q=1, and the text does not say what changes for a known propensity other than 1/2. (c) Binary Y and S are treated as notation rather than restrictions. (d) The known floor q is used both to select the estimator branch and to set the interval radius. Fix: add a short 'Discussion of the model' subsection after the law-class definition that says, for each restriction, where it enters and whether it is believed to be essential or a convenience.

The mechanism that makes dimension matter under known randomization is not given a self-contained intuition. With known propensities and complete data the problem is parametric, so the reader needs a clear statement that the difficulty comes entirely from the bias of the arrived-only contrast, 2*sum_j eps_j w_j eta_j, a functional of products of missing mass and cell means over sparsely observed cells. The current post-theorem paragraph ('reflects the estimator's use of cell corrections') explains the rate through the estimator rather than through the problem. Fix: put this bias decomposition (now buried in step 3 of the upper-risk proof) in the introduction or immediately after the point-risk theorem, and tie it to the Zeng et al. unknown-propensity functional to explain the shared (d/(n log n))^2 shape.

Positioning leans on unpublished self-citations and under-specifies the technical novelty relative to Zeng et al. and Wu and Yang. CausalSmith2026 and CausalSmith2026Annotation are cited without locators as 'direct precedents'. The claimed novelty of the converse ('exactly normalized', 'same experiment') is asserted without saying why approximate normalization plus a Poissonization reduction, as in Zeng et al. Appendix C.5, would not suffice here. In addition, for n below the threshold N_beta the converse proof uses a two-point parametric pair, not the paired priors the introduction describes. Fix: give locators for the self-citations, state in one or two sentences what exact normalization buys (or concede it is a formalization convenience), and note in the introduction that the paired-prior construction operates for n above a beta-dependent threshold with a two-point construction below it.
